{{external media | width= 210px | float= right | headerimage= |video1= [https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/video/can-we-cool-the-planet/ "Can We Cool the Planet?"], ''[[Nova (American TV program)|Nova]]'', October 28, 2020 | video4= [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2pxT-X7L2BI "Patient Geoengineering"], talk to the [[Long Now Foundation]], May 10, 2020 | video2= [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q76t47E1FUA "Solar Geoengineering: Public Policy and Geopolitical Considerations"], talk to the [[Institute of International and European Affairs|IIEA]], September 25, 2019 |video3= {{YouTube|id=EnNerOVUOdo|title="As planet warms, scientists explore 'far out' ways to reduce atmospheric CO2"}}, ''[[PBS NewsHour]]'' March 27, 2019 (with animation of SCoPEx) }}

'''David W. Keith''' is a professor in the Department of the Geophysical Sciences at the University of Chicago. He joined the University of Chicago in April 2023. Keith previously served as the Gordon McKay Professor of [[Applied physics|Applied Physics]] for [[Harvard University]]'s [[Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences|Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences]] (SEAS) and professor of [[public policy]] for the [[John F. Kennedy School of Government|Harvard Kennedy School]] at Harvard University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=David Keith |url=https://www.hks.harvard.edu/faculty/david-keith |access-date=2015-09-30 |publisher=Harvard Kennedy School}}</ref> 
Early contributions include development of the first [[atom interferometer]] (considered a major breakthrough in atomic physics) and a [[Fourier-transform spectroscopy|Fourier-transform spectrometer]] used by [[NASA]] to measure [[atmospheric temperature]] and radiation transfer from space. 

A specialist on energy technology, climate science, and related public policy,<ref name="Kintisch"/> and a pioneer in [[Carbon dioxide removal|carbon capture and storage]],<ref name="Timeline"/> Keith was a founder and board member of [[Carbon Engineering]], it was sold to Occidental in 2023, at which point he was not a board member and had 4% ownership of the company.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Radical - Engineering the Climate: Can Injecting Chemicals in the Sky Help Save the Planet? (Professor David Keith) - BBC Sounds |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sounds/play/m002z79b |access-date=2026-08-17 |website=BBC |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Our Team |url=https://carbonengineering.com/our-team/ |access-date=2015-09-30 |website=Carbon Engineering}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

Keith's research spans multiple fields, including climate-related technology assessment and [[policy analysis]], technology development, [[atmospheric sciences]], and physics.
He strongly advocates for research into geoengineering approaches for addressing climate change, including both [[carbon cycle engineering]]<ref name="Vidal">{{Cite news |last=Vidal |first=John |date=4 February 2018 |title=How Bill Gates aims to clean up the planet |language=en |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2018/feb/04/carbon-emissions-negative-emissions-technologies-capture-storage-bill-gates |access-date=7 February 2018}}</ref> and [[solar radiation management]] approaches.<ref name="Powell">{{cite web |last1=Powell |first1=Alvin |title=Expert: Lift taboo on Earth engineering |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2009/09/earth-engineering/ |website=Harvard Gazette |date= September 23, 2009 |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref> He emphasizes that their scientific, environmental, geopolitical, social, psychological and ethical implications all need to be carefully examined and understood, before there can be a meaningful consideration of their possible use.<ref name="Preston">{{cite journal |last1=Preston |first1=Christopher J. |title=Re-Thinking the Unthinkable: Environmental Ethics and the Presumptive Argument Against Geoengineering |journal=Environmental Values |date=1 November 2011 |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=457–479 |doi=10.3197/096327111X13150367351212 |bibcode=2011EnvV...20..457P |url=http://www.cas.umt.edu/facultydatabase/FILES_Faculty/684/preston.rethinking_the_unthinkable.2011.pdf |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Keith was born in Wisconsin, where his father, a British-born field biologist and [[Canadian Wildlife Service]] civil servant named Anthony Keith, attended grad school. His mother, Deborah Gorham, was a history professor at [[Carleton University]]. Keith grew up in [[Great Britain]] and in [[Ottawa]], [[Ontario]].<ref name="Bergman"/> His stepmother was a biologist, like his father.<ref name="Bergman"/><ref name="Stavins">{{cite web |last1=Stavins |first1=Rob |title=The potential promises and pitfalls of solar geoengineering: A conversation with David Keith |url=https://heep.hks.harvard.edu/files/heep/files/david_keith_environmental_insights_podcast_transcript_2.0_2.7.2020.pdf |website=Environmental Insights |date=February 7, 2020 |publisher=Harvard Environmental Economics Program |access-date=2 July 2021}}</ref><ref name="Montlake"/> Keith is a citizen of Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom.<ref name="CV"/>

He enjoyed reading and [[birdwatching]] with his father and later took up cross-country skiing, rock climbing and winter camping.<ref name="Bergman"/> Keith's interest in physics was strengthened by spending several summers working in the National Research Council laser lab of experimental physicist [[Paul Corkum]], beginning around the end of high school.<ref name="Bergman"/> In 1986 Keith graduated with a B.S. in physics from the [[University of Toronto]].<ref name="Montlake"/>

He developed a love of the Arctic when he spent part of a gap year between undergraduate and graduate studies as a wildlife biologist's research assistant<ref name="Stavins"/> on [[Devon Island]] in [[Nunavut]]. Since then he has canoed on the [[Yellowknife River]], hiked [[Holman Island]] and crossed rough [[sea ice]] from [[Iglulik]] to [[Arctic Bay]] on skis.<ref name="Bergman"/>

==Academic career==
In 1991, Keith earned his doctorate from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in the field of Experimental Physics.<ref name="Montlake">{{cite news |last1=Montlake |first1=Simon |title=Should we fiddle with Earth's thermostat? This man might know how. |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/Environment/2020/0123/Should-we-fiddle-with-Earth-s-thermostat-This-man-might-know-how |work=[[The Christian Science Monitor]] |date=23 January 2020}}</ref> 
As a doctoral student at MIT, Keith was supervised by [[David E. Pritchard]]. Keith was a leader in the research group that created the first working [[atom interferometer]], considered a major breakthrough in atomic physics.<ref name="Rotman"/> This work was the basis for his Ph.D. thesis, ''An Interferometer for Atoms'' (1991).<ref name="PHD">{{cite journal |last1=Keith |first1=David William |title=An Interferometer for Atoms |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=1991 |volume=66 |issue=21 |pages=2693–2696 |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.66.2693 |pmid=10043592 |bibcode=1991PhRvL..66.2693K |url=https://keith.seas.harvard.edu/files/tkg/files/00.keith_.1991.aninterferometerforatomsthesis.x.pdf |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref> After achieving this success, Keith chose to leave atomic physics, in part because one of the most obvious applications for atom interferometry was in building highly accurate [[gyroscopes]] for [[SSBN|submarines carrying ballistic missiles]].<ref name="Rotman">{{cite journal |last1=Rotman |first1=David |title=A Cheap and Easy Plan to Stop Global Warming |journal=MIT Technology Review |date=February 8, 2013 |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2013/02/08/84239/a-cheap-and-easy-plan-to-stop-global-warming/ |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref> 

Keith was a post-doctoral fellow at [[Carnegie Mellon University]] from 1991 to 1992, working with Granger Morgan to better understand uncertainty and expert judgments relating to climate change.<ref name="Stavins"/> Keith became an adjunct assistant professor there in 1992, though working primarily elsewhere.<ref name="NRC"/><ref name="CV"/>
He received a [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] (NOAA) Global Change Fellowship for 1992–1994, which he used to work on [[climate modeling]] at the [[National Center for Atmospheric Research]] (NCAR) in [[Boulder, Colorado]].<ref name="CPAESS">{{cite web |title=C&GC Alumni Class 2 |url=https://cpaess.ucar.edu/cgc/class-2 |website=Cooperative Programs for the Advancement of Earth System Science (CPAESS) |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref>

Keith spent the final year of his NOAA postdoc as a research scientist in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at [[Harvard University]] where he remained from 1993 to 1999. He worked with atmospheric chemist [[James G. Anderson]].<ref name="NRC">{{cite book |last1=((National Research Council, Division on Earth and Life Studies, Board on Chemical Sciences and Technology, Chemical Sciences Roundtable)) |title=Carbon Management: Implications for R&D in the Chemical Sciences and Technology |date=August 15, 2001 |publisher=National Academies Press |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=216–217 |isbn=978-0-309-17066-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PBr_u72EgrEC&pg=PT228}}</ref><ref name="Kintisch">{{cite journal |last1=Kintisch |first1=Eli |title=Dr. Cool |journal=Science |date=18 October 2013 |volume=342 |issue=6156 |pages=307–309 |doi=10.1126/science.342.6156.307 |pmid=24136948 |bibcode=2013Sci...342..307K |url=https://law.uh.edu/faculty/thester/courses/Climate-Change-2013/David%20Keith%20profile.pdf |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="Stavins"/>
Keith was the lead scientist in developing a [[Fourier-transform spectroscopy|Fourier-transform spectrometer]] with high radiometric accuracy which was used by NASA's high-altitude ER-2 research aircraft and by the Arrhenius satellite. Keith's sensors supported the measurement of [[atmospheric temperature]] and radiation transfer from space.<ref name="NAP2007">{{cite book |last1=((National Research Council, Division on Earth and Life Studies, Board on Atmospheric Sciences and Climate, Committee to Review the U.S. Climate Change Science Program's Synthesis and Assessment Product 5.2)) |title=Review of the U.S. Climate Change Science Program's Synthesis and Assessment Product 5.2, "Best Practice Approaches for Characterizing, Communicating, and Incorporating Scientific Uncertainty in Climate Decision Making" |date=March 23, 2007 |publisher=National Academies Press |location=Washington, D.C. |isbn=978-0-309-10570-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EOxTAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA43 |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref><ref name="Anderson">{{cite book |last1=Anderson |first1=James G. |title=Clouds and Water Vapor in the Climate System: Remotely Piloted Aircraft and Satellites |date=Oct 1, 1999 |publisher=NASA |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19990100618/downloads/19990100618.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Keith |first1=David W. |last2=Anderson |first2=James G. |title=Accurate Spectrally Resolved Infrared Radiance Observation from Space: Implications for the Detection of Decade-to-Century–Scale Climatic Change |journal=Journal of Climate |date=1 March 2001 |volume=14 |issue=5 |pages=979–990 |doi=10.1175/1520-0442(2001)014<0979:ASRIRO>2.0.CO;2 |bibcode=2001JCli...14..979K |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/238554758 |access-date=1 July 2021|doi-access=free }}</ref>

As of 1999, Keith became an assistant professor at the [[Engineering and Public Policy|Department of Engineering and Public Policy]] at Carnegie Mellon University.<ref name="NRC"/><ref name="CV"/> By 2000, Keith and Ph.D. student James Rhodes were developing a framework for what would be called [[bioenergy with carbon capture and storage]] (BECCS). From the beginning, Keith has pointed out both advantages and concerns about possible approaches to climate mitigation.<ref name="Timeline">{{cite web |last1=Hickman |first1=Leo |title=Timeline: How BECCS became climate change's 'saviour' technology |url=https://www.carbonbrief.org/beccs-the-story-of-climate-changes-saviour-technology|date=April 13, 2016 |website=CarbonBrief |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="Rhodes">{{cite journal |last1=Keith |first1=David W. |last2=Rhodes |first2=James S. |title=Bury, Burn or Both: A Two-for-One Deal on Biomass Carbon and Energy |journal=Climatic Change |date=2002 |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=375–377 |doi=10.1023/A:1016187420442 |bibcode=2002ClCh...54..375K |s2cid=151157077 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023%2FA%3A1016187420442 |access-date=3 July 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2004, Keith was recruited to join the [[University of Calgary]], where he became a professor of chemical and petroleum engineering and economics, and held the [[Canada Research Chair]] in Energy and the Environment. Keith became the director of the Institute for Sustainable Energy, Environment and Economy (ISEEE)'s Energy and Environmental Systems Group at the University of Calgary, an interdisciplinary research group within ISEEE.<ref name="Lowey">{{cite journal |last1=Lowey |first1=Mark |title=ISEEE – A Unique Model to Advance Sustainable Energy Technologies |journal=Recorder |date=2005|publisher= Canadian Society of Exploration Geophysicists |volume=30 |issue=7 |url=https://csegrecorder.com/articles/view/iseee-a-unique-model-to-advance-sustainable-energy-technologies |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref> While at the University of Calgary, he remained an adjunct professor at Carnegie Mellon.<ref name="CV"/> 
At ISEEE, Keith sought to build connections between government, academics, environmentalists and business people. He gained the support of four major energy sector executives, publishing a 2007 report promoting carbon capture and storage.<ref name="Kintisch"/> 

Keith later felt that the intellectual integrity of the organization became compromised.<ref name="Kintisch"/><ref name="CBC2013"/>
Effective September 1, 2011, Keith resigned from the University of Calgary. He remained an adjunct professor in the Physics and Astronomy Department at the University of Calgary, and a visiting fellow at ISEEE.<ref name="CBC2013">{{cite news |title=Scientist calls U of C energy centre a failure |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/scientist-calls-u-of-c-energy-centre-a-failure-1.1337139 |access-date=30 June 2021 |work=CBC News |date=January 28, 2013}}</ref> 

Also as of 2011, Keith accepted a professorship in applied physics and public policy at the [[Kennedy School]] of [[Harvard University]].<ref name="CBC2013"/>
In 2017 Keith was a founding co-director, with climate economist [[Gernot Wagner]], of Harvard's Solar Geoengineering Research Program.<ref name="Ramachandran">{{cite news|last1=Ramachandran|first1=Akshitha|title=Harvard Researchers Launch Solar Geoengineering Moonshot|url=http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2017/4/17/solar-geoengineering-program-launch/|access-date=19 December 2017|work=[[The Harvard Crimson]] |date=17 April 2017}}</ref> As of 2019, Keith became the sole director, after Wagner joined the faculty of [[New York University]].<ref name="Cohen">{{cite news |last1=Cohen |first1=Joyce |title=They Wanted a Downtown Loft With Few Walls. Which One Would You Choose? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/09/05/realestate/05hunt-wagner.html |access-date=3 July 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 5, 2019}}</ref>

Keith presented to US [[National Academy of Sciences]] meetings in 2000, 2009 and 2013.

Keith moved his research to the University of Chicago in 2023, where he will lead a program with up to ten faculty members studying geoengineering.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Gelles |first=David |date=2024-08-01 |title=This Scientist Has a Risky Plan to Cool Earth. There's Growing Interest. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/01/climate/david-keith-solar-geoengineering.html |access-date=2024-08-10 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

==Public policy==

Keith was a coauthor of the 2001 [[IPCC Third Assessment Report]]<ref name="AR5">{{cite web |title=Contributions: AR5 Page |url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/report/ar5/authors.php?s=Keith |website=IPCC Home |access-date=3 July 2021}}</ref> 
(chapters AR3-WG1, 8 Model Evaluation;<ref>{{cite book |last1=IPCC |title=Climate Change 2001: Mitigation, Contribution of Working Group III to the Third Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK |chapter=8. Model Evaluation |page=471 |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/WGI_TAR_full_report.pdf |access-date=3 July 2021}}</ref>
AR3-WG3, 4 Technological and Economic Potential of Options to Enhance, Maintain, and Manage Biological Carbon Reservoirs and Geo-engineering<ref>{{cite book |author=IPCC |title=Climate Change 2001: Mitigation, Contribution of Working Group III to the Third Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK |chapter= 4. Technological and Economic Potential of Options to Enhance, Maintain, and Manage Biological Carbon Reservoirs and Geo-engineering |page=301 |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/WGIII_TAR_full_report.pdf |access-date=3 July 2021}}</ref>).
Keith also chaired one of three groups for the [[United Nations]]' [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC)<ref name="Lowey"/> and was a lead author of the 2005 ''IPCC Special Report on Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage''.<ref name="IPCC2005">{{cite book |last1=Metz |first1=Bert |last2=Davidson |first2=Ogunlade |last3=de Coninck |first3=Heleen |last4=Loos |first4=Manuela |last5=Meyer |first5=Leo |title=IPCC Special Report on Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage |date=2005 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |page=418 |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/report/carbon-dioxide-capture-and-storage/ |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref>
He resigned from the committee for the [[IPCC Fifth Assessment Report]].<ref name="Goodell">{{cite magazine |last1=Goodell |first1=Jeff |title=Global Warming Is Very Real Scientists are fighting deniers with irrefutable proof the planet is headed for catastrophe |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-news/global-warming-is-very-real-179487/ |access-date=8 July 2021 |magazine=Rolling Stone |date=September 12, 2013}}</ref>

In May 2005 Keith was appointed to a federal advisory panel for the Canadian government's Sustainable Energy Science and Technology Strategy. 
Keith was a member of the ''Geoengineering the climate: science, governance and uncertainty'' working group of the UK [[Royal Society]], which produced a 2009 report.<ref name=rs09>{{cite news |url=https://royalsociety.org/~/media/Royal_Society_Content/policy/publications/2009/8693.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721043235/https://royalsociety.org/~/media/Royal_Society_Content/policy/publications/2009/8693.pdf |archive-date=July 21, 2015 |title=Geoengineering the climate: science, governance and uncertainty |date=2009}}</ref><ref name="RS">{{cite web |title=Sept. 1: Carnegie Mellon Adjunct Professor David Keith Studies Geoengineering as Tool To Limit Extreme Climate Change |url=https://www.cmu.edu/news/archive/2009/September/sept1_geoengineering.shtml |website=Carnegie Mellon University |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref> 
In 2010, Keith testified before committees of the [[US Congress]]<ref name="Congress2010">{{cite book |author=United States. Congress. House. Committee on Science and Technology |title=Engineering the climate: research needs and strategies for international coordination |date=2010 |publisher=U.S. G.P.O. |location=Washington |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CPRT-111HPRT62619/html/CPRT-111HPRT62619.htm |access-date=3 July 2021}}</ref> and the [[UK Parliament]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Regulation of Geoengineering - Science and Technology Committee |url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200910/cmselect/cmsctech/221/10011304.htm |website=UK Parliament |access-date=3 July 2021}}</ref>

With [[Ken Caldeira]], Keith has managed the Fund for Innovative Energy and Climate Research (FICER), established by [[Bill Gates]] for climate-change research.<ref name="O'Donnell"/><ref name="Kintisch"/>

Keith was one of 18 members of the Washington, D.C. [[Bipartisan Policy Center]] (BPC)'s Task Force on Climate Remediation, which released a research report on October 4, 2011.<ref name=bpc>{{Cite web |title=Blue Ribbon Task Force on Climate Remediation Releases Report Calling for Federal Geo-Engineering Research Program |url=https://bipartisanpolicy.org/press-release/blue-ribbon-task-force-climate-remediation-releases-report-calling-feder/ |date=October 4, 2011 |publisher=Bipartisan Policy Center |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref> The authors of the BPC report believe "the (US) federal government should embark on a focused and systematic program of research into climate remediation."<ref name=bpc/> As of 2021, the [[National Academies]] issued a report on the same subject, supporting a robust research plan and substantial oversight, risk assessment, and public outreach efforts and describing a framework for governance of possible experiments. Keith sees its governance recommendations as "actionable, incremental, and well-reasoned".<ref name="Voosen">{{cite journal |last1=Voosen |first1=Paul |title=U.S. needs solar geoengineering research program, National Academies says |journal=Science |date=25 March 2021 |doi=10.1126/science.abi7089 |s2cid=233702289 |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/us-needs-solar-geoengineering-research-program-national-academies-says |access-date=7 July 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Scientific work==
Keith has written about the possible cost-effectiveness and geopolitical and ethical implications of many approaches to climate change and climate mitigation. In 2003, he and Alexander Farrell published a commentary in ''Science'', questioning government initiatives for the development of [[fuel cell vehicle]]s using [[compressed hydrogen]]. Hydrogen tends to be derived from oil and coal, and produces carbon dioxide.<ref name="Hoffmann">{{cite news |last1=Hoffmann |first1=Karen |title=Debunking the hype of hydrogen cars |url=https://old.post-gazette.com/healthscience/20030728hydrogencars0728p2.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150220002146/http://old.post-gazette.com/healthscience/20030728hydrogencars0728p2.asp |url-status=dead |archive-date=20 February 2015 |access-date=3 July 2021 |work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |date=July 28, 2003}}</ref>
In 2004, the National Academy of Sciences published a controversial paper in which his computer models suggested that massive wind farms turbines might have unexpected local and global impacts on climate. His argument was not that wind energy should not be considered, but rather that it needed to be better understood.<ref name="Bergman"/>
After early skepticism in 2008-2011 about solar energy's potential to become competitive, he now sees solar power as a leading contender for providing energy without huge environmental impact.<ref name="Fialka">{{cite journal |last1=Fialka |first1=John |title=Are We Entering the Photovoltaic Energy Era? |journal=Scientific American |date=December 15, 2016 |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-we-entering-the-photovoltaic-energy-era/ |access-date=3 July 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Keith |first=David |date=April 28, 2016 |title=I Was Wrong About the Limits of Solar. PV Is Becoming Dirt Cheap |work=Greentech Media |url=https://www.greentechmedia.com/articles/read/i-was-wrong-about-the-economic-limitations-of-solar-power |access-date=7 February 2018}}</ref>

===Carbon engineering===
In the 1990s and 2000s, Keith worked on [[Carbon capture and storage|CO<sub>2</sub> capture and storage]],<ref name="Bergman"/> considering it in terms of technology, economics and regulatory policy in the energy industry.<ref name="Stavins"/><ref name="Roundtable">{{cite book |last1=Keith |first1=David |editor=National Research Council (US) |title=Chemical Sciences Roundtable. Carbon Management: Implications for R&D in the Chemical Sciences and Technology: A Workshop Report to the Chemical Sciences Roundtable |chapter=8, Industrial Carbon Management: An Overview |date=2001 |publisher=National Academies Press (US) |location=Washington (DC) |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK44136/ |access-date=7 July 2021}}</ref> Keith emphasizes that the primary goal in combating climate change must be the reduction of carbon emissions. However, it will still be necessary to counteract the effects of the carbon dioxide that has already been released into the atmosphere. He therefore sees multiple approaches to the problem of climate change, including pollution-management techniques and a "carbon tax", as desirable.<ref name="Bergman"/> He has been criticized by environmental groups, politicians and energy-related business people for different recommendations.<ref name="Bergman"/> 

As of 2005, Keith's team at the University of Calgary built a five-metre tower to test the feasibility of removing "scrubbing" CO<sub>2</sub> from the air and storing it underground.<ref name="Bergman"/> 
In 2009 Keith founded [[Carbon Engineering]], which seeks to develop technologies for the removal of [[carbon dioxide]] from the [[air]] and its conversion into pure CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref name=tollefson18/><ref name="Stavins"/><ref name="Vidal"/><ref name="Eisenberg">{{cite news|last1=Eisenberg|first1=Anne|title=Pulling Carbon Dioxide Out of Thin Air|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/06/business/pilot-plant-in-the-works-for-carbon-dioxide-cleansing.html?_r=1&|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=3 December 2015|date=2013-01-05}}</ref><ref name="guntherguardian">{{cite web|last1=Gunther|first1=Marc|title=The business of cooling the planet|url=http://fortune.com/2011/10/07/the-business-of-cooling-the-planet/|website=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]] |publisher=Time Inc.|date=7 October 2011}}</ref>
Having created the company, he largely ceased to do research and policy analysis in that area, feeling it would be a conflict of interest.<ref name="Stavins"/>

As of October 2015, Carbon Engineering opened a demonstration plant for direct-air CO<sub>2</sub> capture, in [[Squamish, British Columbia]]. The company hopes to use the carbon dioxide extracted from the air to produce an energy-dense synthetic carbon-based fuel, suitable for semis, buses and aircraft. Ideally they would like to produce a fuel that is economical, carbon-based and carbon-neutral.<ref name=thts>{{cite web|last1=Hamilton|first1=Tyler|title=Snatching CO2 back from the air|url=https://www.thestar.com/business/2015/10/08/snatching-co2-back-from-the-air.html|website=[[Toronto Star]]|date=8 October 2015}}</ref> Financial backers of Carbon Engineering include [[Bill Gates]], [[N. Murray Edwards]],<ref name="Hamilton">{{cite news |last1=Hamilton |first1=Tyler |title=Out of Thin Air |url=https://www.cheminst.ca/magazine/article/out-of-thin-air/ |access-date=7 July 2021 |work=The Chemical Institute of Canada |date=November 2016}}</ref> Peter J. Thomson, [[Chevron Corporation]], [[Occidental Petroleum]], and mining conglomerate [[BHP]].<ref name=cegm>{{cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-bcs-carbon-engineering-secures-68-million-to-commercialize-c0/|title=B.C.'s Carbon Engineering secures $68-million to commercialize CO2-removal technology|last1=Silcoff|first1=Sean|date=21 March 2019|work=The Globe and Mail|access-date=24 September 2019}}</ref> Occidental purchased the company in 2023 for $1.1 billion; Keith held about four percent ownership prior to the sale.<ref name=":0" />

===Solar geoengineering===
Keith has worked on [[solar radiation management|solar geoengineering]] since 1992, when he and Hadi Dowlatabadi published one of the first assessments of the technology and its policy implications, introducing a structured comparison of cost and risk. Keith has consistently argued that geoengineering needs a "systematic research program" to determine whether or not its approaches are feasible.<ref name="Kintisch"/><ref name="O'Donnell"/><ref name=keith92>{{Cite journal |last1=Keith |first1=David W. |last2=Dowlatabadi |first2=Hadi |date=July 7, 1992 |title=A Serious Look at Geoengineering |url=http://keith.seas.harvard.edu/papers/09_Keith_1992_SeriousLookAtGeoeng_s.pdf |journal=Eos, Transactions American Geophysical Union |volume=73 |issue=27 |pages=289 and 292–293 |bibcode=1992EOSTr..73..289K |doi=10.1029/91eo00231 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001044817/http://keith.seas.harvard.edu/papers/09_Keith_1992_SeriousLookAtGeoeng_s.pdf |archive-date=October 1, 2015 |access-date=2015-09-30}}</ref> 
Keith has also appealed for international standards of governance and oversight for how such research might proceed.<ref name="Lieberman">{{cite news|last1=Lieberman|first1=Bruce|title=Geoengineering: crazy...with a big 'but' |url=https://www.yaleclimateconnections.org/2016/11/geoengineering-crazy-for-sure-but-with-a-big-but|access-date=5 February 2018|work=[[Yale Climate Connections]]|date=2 November 2016}}</ref> 

Keith published another overview of geoengineering in 2000, describing it in terms of [[moral hazard]] and setting [[geoengineering]] in the context of the post-war history of [[weather control]]. At the time geoengineering was "deeply controversial" and rarely talked about. Since then, interest in the field has increased and it is more openly discussed.<ref name="Mason"/><ref name="O'Donnell">{{cite news |last1=O'Donnell |first1=Erin |title=Buffering the Sun: David Keith and the question of climate engineering |url=https://www.harvardmagazine.com/2013/07/buffering-the-sun |access-date=7 July 2021 |work=[[Harvard Magazine]] |issue=July-August |date=2013}}</ref><ref name="Keith">{{cite journal |last1=Keith |first1=David W. |title=Geoengineering the climate: History and Prospect |journal=Annual Review of Energy and the Environment |date=November 2000 |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=245–284 |doi=10.1146/annurev.energy.25.1.245 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 

Related publications include:
* in 2010 a method to reduce the amount of [[sulfur]] needed for a given [[radiative forcing]];<ref name=keith10a>{{Cite journal |last1=Pierce |first1=Jeffrey R. |last2=Weisenstein |first2=Debra K. |last3=Heckendorn |first3=Patricia |last4=Peter |first4=Thomas |last5=Keith |first5=David W. |date=2010 |title=Efficient formation of stratospheric aerosol for climate engineering by emission of condensible vapor from aircraft |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=37 |issue=18 |pages=L18805 |bibcode=2010GeoRL..3718805P |doi=10.1029/2010GL043975 |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11850/23356 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> 
* in 2010 a proposal for self-levitating [[photophoretic]] particles that might limit [[ozone]] loss;<ref name=keith10b>{{Cite journal |last=Keith |first=D. W. |year=2010 |title=Photophoretic levitation of engineered aerosols for geoengineering |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=107 |issue=38 |pages=16428–16431 |bibcode=2010PNAS..10716428K |doi=10.1073/pnas.1009519107 |pmc=2944714 |pmid=20823254|doi-access=free }}</ref>
* in 2011 he co-authored the first large-scale survey of public perception as to [[geoengineering]];<ref name=keith11>{{Cite journal |last1=Mercer |first1=A. M. |last2=Keith |first2=D. W. |last3=Sharp |first3=J. D. |date=2011-10-24 |title=Public understanding of solar radiation management - IOPscience |journal=Environmental Research Letters |volume=6 |issue=4 |article-number=044006 |bibcode=2011ERL.....6d4006M |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/6/4/044006 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* in 2012 the first quantitative analysis of "regional inequality" of "[[solar radiation management]]";<ref name=keith12>{{Cite journal |last1=Moreno-Cruz |first1=Juan B. |last2=Ricke |first2=Katharine L. |last3=Keith |first3=David W. |year=2012 |title=A simple model to account for regional inequalities in the effectiveness of solar radiation management |journal=Climatic Change |volume=110 |issue=3–4 |pages=649–668 |doi=10.1007/s10584-011-0103-z|bibcode=2012ClCh..110..649M |s2cid=18903547 }}</ref>
* he supervised the first economics Ph.D. to focus on geoengineering, and together with his student Moreno-Cruz in 2012 published an economic analysis of "optimal" decisions under result uncertainty.<ref name="harvard1" /><ref name="springer1">{{Cite journal |last1=Moreno-Cruz |first1=Juan B. |last2=Keith |first2=David W. |date=2012-05-17 |title=Climate policy under uncertainty: a case for solar geoengineering |journal=Climatic Change |volume=121 |issue=3 |pages=431–444 |doi=10.1007/s10584-012-0487-4 |doi-access=free|hdl=1853/44253 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* in 2013 he proposed a two-threshold system that combines "deployment moratoria" with a pathway for regulating "small-scale" (sic) research;<ref name=keith13>{{Cite journal |last1=Parson |first1=Edward A. |last2=Keith |first2=David W. |year=2013 |title=End the Deadlock on Governance of Geoengineering Research |url=http://keith.seas.harvard.edu/papers/163.Parson.Keith.DeadlockOnGonvernance.p.pdf |journal=Science |publisher=Keith.seas.harvard.edu |volume=339 |issue=6125 |pages=1278–9 |bibcode=2013Sci...339.1278P |doi=10.1126/science.1232527 |pmid=23493699 |s2cid=206546509 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304105817/http://keith.seas.harvard.edu/papers/163.Parson.Keith.DeadlockOnGonvernance.p.pdf |archive-date=2016-03-04 |access-date=2015-09-30}}</ref><ref name="harvard1">{{Cite web |title=Solar Geoenginering |url=http://www.keith.seas.harvard.edu/geo-engineering/ |access-date=2015-09-30 |publisher=David Keith |archive-date=10 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910070130/http://www.keith.seas.harvard.edu/geo-engineering/ }}</ref>

====''A Case for Climate Engineering''====
In 2013, Keith published ''A Case for Climate Engineering'', providing "a clear and accessible overview" to a "controversial technology".<ref>{{cite web |title=A Case for Climate Engineering David Keith |url=http://bostonreview.net/br-book/case-climate-engineering |website=Boston Review|date=October 28, 2013 |access-date=8 July 2021}}</ref> The book is described as a useful entry point for discussions, particularly for [[stratospheric aerosol injection]] and less so for other approaches to geoengineering. "The book's arguments are clear and it is upfront about many of the problems that arise from the position it defends."<ref name="Markusson">{{cite journal |last1=Markusson |first1=Nils |title=Book Review: A Case for Climate Engineering, written by David Keith |journal=Climate Law |date=23 February 2014 |volume=4 |issue=3–4 |pages=365–368 |doi=10.1163/18786561-00404011 |bibcode=2014ClimL...4..365M |url=https://brill.com/view/journals/clla/4/3-4/article-p365_11.xml?language=en |access-date=8 July 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
Another reviewer appreciated Keith's ability to discuss issues "in simple language that can be understood by any reader" and his objectivity as he "discusses his own internal dilemma" and "exposes the reader to opposing views".<ref name="Silverstein">{{cite news |last1=Silverstein |first1=Barry |title=A Case for Climate Engineering David Keith |url=https://www.forewordreviews.com/reviews/a-case-for-climate-engineering/ |access-date=8 July 2021 |work=Foreword Reviews |date=2014}}</ref>

{{quote|A leading scientist long concerned about climate change, Keith offers no naïve proposal for an easy fix to what is perhaps the most challenging question of our time; climate engineering is no silver bullet. But he argues that after decades during which very little progress has been made in reducing carbon emissions we must put this technology on the table and consider it responsibly.<ref name="Hansman">{{cite journal |last1=Hansman |first1=Heather |title=Is This Plan to Combat Climate Change Insane or Insanely Genius? |journal=[[Smithsonian (magazine)|Smithsonian]] |date=May 14, 2015 |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/is-this-plan-combat-climate-change-insane-insanely-genius-180955258/ |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref> }}

The book garnered the attention of [[Stephen Colbert]], and Keith appeared in a 9 December 2013 segment on ''[[The Colbert Report]]'' to discuss his geoengineering idea to slow climate change by spraying reflective particles into the upper atmosphere.<ref name=colbert>{{Cite web |title=David Keith |url=http://www.cc.com/video-clips/lv0hd2/the-colbert-report-david-keith |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001040231/http://www.cc.com/video-clips/lv0hd2/the-colbert-report-david-keith |archive-date=1 October 2015 |access-date=2015-09-30 |publisher=Comedy Central}}</ref><ref name="imdb">{{cite news |title=The Colbert Report (2005–2014) - David Keith |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3363014/ |publisher=IMDb |date=9 December 2013}}</ref> Keith described the possibility of deploying planes to release tons of [[sulfuric acid]] into the atmosphere, which he freely admitted "would be a totally imperfect technical fix&nbsp;.. But it might actually save people and be useful."<ref name="West">{{cite journal |last1=West |first1=James |title=Will Colbert Use "The Late Show" To Save the World? |journal=Mother Jones |date=April 11, 2014 |url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2014/04/stephen-colbert-climate-change-cbs/ |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref> Colbert was skeptical. Critics of the idea also include [[University of Chicago]] geophysicist [[Raymond Pierrehumbert]] who termed the idea "wildly, utterly, howlingly barking mad",<ref name="Montlake"/> and the ''[[USA Today]]'' editorial board.<ref name="usato">{{cite news |author=USA Today Editorial Board |title=Geoengineering won't solve climate change: One View |type=Editorial opinion |url=https://www.rgj.com/story/opinion/voices/2015/02/19/geoengineering-solve-climate-change-one-view/23653841/ |work=[[Reno Gazette-Journal]] |date=18 February 2015}}</ref>

====SCoPEx====
Keith has worked initially with atmospheric chemist James G. Anderson<ref name="tollefson18"/>
and later with principal investigator [[Frank Keutsch]] in the "sun-dimming" project [[SCoPEx]], to examine the potential of seeding the [[stratosphere]] with reflective particles that would direct [[sunlight]] away from the earth. The idea was inspired by natural events such as the volcanic eruption of [[Mount Pinatubo]], which released sulfur and other particles into the air and caused a decrease in temperatures worldwide.<ref name="Mason"/>

Computer models suggest that a particle dispersion approach could reduce solar wattage and ambient temperatures.<ref name="tollefson18">{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/d41586-018-07533-4|doi-access=free|title=First sun-dimming experiment will test a way to cool Earth|year=2018|last1=Tollefson |first1=Jeff |journal=Nature|volume=563|issue=7733|pages=613–615|pmid=30479388|bibcode=2018Natur.563..613T}}</ref>
Types of particles that have been proposed include [[sulfur dioxide]], [[diamond]] dust, [[alumina]] and [[calcite]] or other forms of [[calcium carbonate]].<ref name="Temple">{{Cite web | first1=James |last1= Temple |date=March 24, 2017 |title=Harvard Scientists Moving Ahead on Plans for Atmospheric Geoengineering Experiment |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/603974/harvard-scientists-moving-ahead-on-plans-for-atmospheric-geoengineering-experiments/ |access-date=2017-12-19 |work=[[MIT Technology Review]]}}</ref><ref name="Mason"/> Major concerns for such an approach include the questions of how long particles would remain in the stratosphere, how they might interact with other components of the atmosphere, and whether they would increase pollution, cause health risks for humans, or have other negative ecological effects.<ref name="Mason"/><ref name="tollefson18"/>

An early step in the project would be a small test using a [[balloon]] to release a small amount -- perhaps a kilogram -- of a chemical in the stratosphere. By studying local effects scientists could gain a better understanding of how the particles and the stratosphere would behave, to better assess the idea's feasibility and risks. Sensors attached to the balloon's gondola could measure particle reflectivity, degree of dispersion or coalescence of the plume, and interactions with other components of the atmosphere. If carried out, it would be one of the first official geoengineering-related experiments to be conducted outside of the laboratory.<ref name="Mason">{{Cite magazine |first1= Betsy |last1= Mason |title=Why solar geoengineering should be part of the climate crisis solution |url= https://knowablemagazine.org/article/food-environment/2020/why-solar-geoengineering-should-be-part-climate-crisis-solution |magazine=[[Knowable Magazine]] |date=September 16, 2020 |doi=10.1146/knowable-091620-2 | doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Temple"/><ref name="Rotman"/>

A 2012 proposal to carry out such a test in [[New Mexico]], releasing sulphates in the lower stratosphere, was withdrawn. In 2020, the location of another proposed test, using calcium carbonate, was shifted from the U.S. southwest to Sweden, near the Arctic Circle.<ref name="Grossman">{{cite news |last1=Grossman |first1=Daniel |title=Geoengineering: A worst-case Plan B? Or a fuse not to be lit? |url=https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2021/06/geoengineering-a-worst-case-plan-b-or-a-fuse-not-to-be-lit/ |access-date=3 July 2021 |work=Yale Climate Connections |date=June 8, 2021}}</ref>
In February 2021, plans to launch a stratospheric seeder balloon from [[Kiruna]]'s [[Esrange Space Center]] in [[Lapland (Sweden)|Lapland]] ran into opposition from the Swedes who wrote a heated letter to [[Per Bolund]], the Swedish minister for environment and the [[Swedish Space Corporation]] (SSC). The latter said "The flight will only be conducted provided that it is compliant with national and international regulations. The process to find out if this flight is legally compliant and ethically appropriate is ongoing. As of today we don't know whether there will be a flight or not."<ref name="pggnm">{{cite news |last1=Greenfield |first1=Patrick |title=Balloon test flight plan under fire over solar geoengineering fears |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/feb/08/solar-geoengineering-test-flight-plan-under-fire-over-environmental-concerns-aoe |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=8 February 2021}}</ref> On 31 March 2021, the SSC "said it had decided not to conduct the technical test" in the face of opposition from the local [[Sámi people|Sami]] [[reindeer]] herders and other environmental groups such as the [[Swedish Society for Nature Conservation]], who thought the techniques "too dangerous to ever be used".<ref name="Goering">{{cite news|first1=Laurie |last1=Goering |title=Sweden rejects pioneering test of solar geoengineering tech |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-climate-change-geoengineering-sweden-idUSKBN2BN35X |work=[[Reuters]] |date=31 March 2021}}</ref><ref name="nytff">{{cite news |last1=Fountain |first1=Henry |last2=Flavelle |first2=Christopher |title=Test Flight for Sunlight-Blocking Research Is Canceled |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/02/climate/solar-geoengineering-block-sunlight.html |work=The New York Times |date=2 April 2021}}</ref><ref name="tolrb">{{cite news |last1=Blakely |first1=Rhys |title=Space agency ditches Scopex plan to dim the sun with dust |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/article/space-agency-ditches-scopex-plan-to-dim-the-sun-with-dust-bq3j37t5l |work=[[The Times]] |date=8 April 2021}}</ref>

==Media==
Keith is a frequent speaker and presenter. Among others, he has shared his thoughts in the [[TED (conference)|TED forum]] in 2007,<ref name=teddwk>{{Cite web |title=David Keith: A critical look at geoengineering against climate change &#124; TED Talk | date=13 November 2007 |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/david_keith_a_critical_look_at_geoengineering_against_climate_change?language=en |access-date=2015-09-30 |publisher=TED.com}}</ref> 
was featured on the [[Discovery Channel]] in 2008,<ref name=dcdwk>{{Cite web |date=October 23, 2008 |title=Geo-engineering: Removing carbon from air - Discovery Channel |url=http://geo-engineering.blogspot.com/2008/10/removing-carbon-from-air-discovery.html |access-date=2015-09-30 |publisher=Geo-engineering.blogspot.com}}</ref> 
participated in a panel on 21st-century challenges at the [[Royal Geographical Society]] in 2009,<ref>{{cite web |title=Geo-engineering our climate |date=14 May 2009 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JVRer81mlZM  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211220/JVRer81mlZM |archive-date=2021-12-20 |url-status=live|website=Youtube |publisher=Royal Geographical Society |access-date=2 July 2021}}{{cbignore}}</ref>
did an interview on [[BBC News (British TV channel)|BBC News]] ''[[HARDTalk]]'' in 2011,<ref name=bbcdwk>{{Cite web |date=2011-11-14 |title=David Keith, environmental scientist |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b01771jt |access-date=2015-09-30 |work=[[HARDTalk]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-01-22 |title=The original David Keith Interview on BBC Hard talk show Host - Stephen Sackur |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uEiPm-nlN7c  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211220/uEiPm-nlN7c |archive-date=2021-12-20 |url-status=live|access-date=2015-09-30 |publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref> and appeared in a ''[[Nova (American TV program)|Nova]]'' documentary on geoengineering which aired 28 October 2020.<ref name="Nova">{{cite news |title=Can We Cool the Planet? |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/video/can-we-cool-the-planet/ |access-date=2 July 2021 |work=[[Nova (American TV program)|Nova]] |date=October 28, 2020}}</ref>
